changes.before: Change 1750 milliseconds to 2500 milliseconds. What whole-seconds count prints?
changes.after: Convert a time duration while keeping track of its unit.

before: std::chrono::duration represents a count together with a tick period. milliseconds{1750} is not the bare integer 1750 seconds. count() returns the stored count in that duration’s own unit.
duration_cast<seconds> converts this integer millisecond duration to whole seconds. The fractional part is discarded toward zero, so 1750 milliseconds becomes 1 second, not a rounded 2.

For real elapsed timing, subtract two steady_clock::now() time points and convert the resulting duration. A monotonic clock is suited to elapsed time, but workload timings still vary; this deterministic example converts a supplied duration instead of promising a benchmark result.
Expected output or behavior: 1. Local compiler test evidence is recorded separately from app reading completion.

Optional local transfer task: Compare a whole-seconds cast with duration<double> for the same supplied interval; label each output’s unit. You may trace this without a compiler; finishing the reading is not proof of a local run.
after: A duration is an amount of time. std::chrono stores a count together with its unit. milliseconds{1750} means 1,750 milliseconds, not 1,750 seconds. One second contains 1,000 milliseconds.
duration_cast converts between duration types. Converting this integer duration to seconds drops the fractional part toward zero. It does not round to the nearest whole second.
count() returns the number in the duration's own unit. After conversion to seconds, its count is measured in seconds.
The program prints 1. The supplied duration is one and three-quarter seconds, but the whole-second result keeps only one.

For actual elapsed time, subtract two steady_clock::now() time points. That clock does not move backward, which helps measure intervals. This example converts a supplied duration, so its output does not depend on how fast the computer runs.
